articles.title: The grass beneath our feet: Why rangelands matter
articles.summary: In northern Kenya, a herder scans the sky for rain that hasn't come. The grass his animals need is thinning by the day.
articles.content:
He's not alone, from Africa's grasslands to the salt-crusted plains of Central Asia, this same story is playing out for millions of people who depend on land many people may never think about: Rangelands.

What are rangelands and why should we care?

Rangelands, which are found on every continent apart from Antarctica, are the grasslands, shrublands and drylands that don't get farmed in the traditional sense, but nevertheless are a key part of the world's food system.

2 billion people rely on them for food, livestock and livelihoods

rely on them for food, livestock and livelihoods They supply nearly 70 per cent of the world's livestock feed

Yet up to 40 per cent are already degraded or at risk of vanishing, worn down by drought, overgrazing and years of being overlooked

© UNDP

When a rangeland fails, it isn't an abstract environmental loss. It's a family's herd with nothing to eat, a market with fewer animals to sell, a community's food security unravelling in real time.

Three countries, one warning sign

Botswana

Rangelands cover much of this southern African country and underpin its economy, from beef exports to safari tourism.

But until a recent nationwide ecosystem assessment, there was no complete picture of their condition.

The findings were sobering: grasslands are shrinking as invasive plants spread and droughts hit harder and more often, leaving less time for the land to recover.

© UNDP

Encouragingly, the assessment found that where traditional, community-led land governance is still strong, the rangelands hold up better, a reminder that local knowledge is a genuine asset, not a footnote.

Kazakhstan

Once the world's fourth-largest lake, the Aral Sea in Central Asia has largely vanished, leaving a 5.4-million-hectare salt desert behind.

In the neighbouring Kyzylorda region, over 80 per cent of pastures are now degraded, and toxic dust storms carry salt for thousands of kilometres.

It's a stark example of how an environmental disaster in one place can poison land and livelihoods far beyond its borders.

Kenya

Marsabit County in northern Kenya is home to the Chalbi desert. Satellite records dating back to 1990 show grasslands steadily turning to barren ground, with the desert projected to double in size within decades if nothing changes, swallowing the pastures that generations of pastoralist communities have relied on.

What's being done about it

Across all three countries, the response follows a similar, hopeful pattern: pairing hard data with the knowledge of the people who live on the land.

Botswana built its national ecosystem assessment with more than 2,000 contributors, including government bodies, researchers and traditional knowledge holders, creating an evidence base to guide future land policy.

Kazakhstan commissioned a detailed study of the links between climate, land and water, now shaping pasture restoration and irrigation plans, alongside a saxaul tree replanting programme on the dried seabed, already covering 337,000 hectares and aiming for 1.1 million by 2030.

Kenya combined 33 years of satellite data with the memories of Indigenous elders who recall how the land used to look, feeding into practical fixes; a flood-diverting structure in Kalacha, test plots for regrowing vegetation, and training so communities can track changes themselves.

© UNDP

The takeaway

What connects these landscapes, thousands of miles apart, is a simple lesson: restoration sticks when people see their own knowledge and experience reflected in the solution. Data alone doesn't save a rangeland; trust, ownership and lived expertise do.

For the herder still watching the sky, that combination might be the difference between a herd that survives and one that doesn't.

On the road to Ulaanbaatar

The challenges rangelands face are due to be discussed at a UN desertification conference which is being held in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia from 17 August.

The Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services Network (BES-Net) is one of the flagship initiatives of the UN Development Programme Nature Pledge, which focuses on strengthening efforts to protect and restore the Planet.

articles.personality_title: Communities and data join forces to save vital rangelands worldwide
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Rangelands are grasslands, shrublands, and drylands found on every continent except Antarctica. They are not farmed like regular fields but are crucial for feeding livestock and supporting the livelihoods of about 2 billion people worldwide.

**What happened** – In Botswana, Kazakhstan, and Kenya, rangelands are shrinking or degrading due to drought, invasive plants, and human activity. Each country has started large projects combining scientific data and local knowledge to understand and restore these lands. Botswana involved over 2,000 experts and local leaders to assess its ecosystem. Kazakhstan is replanting trees and improving pastures on the dried Aral Sea bed. Kenya uses 33 years of satellite data plus stories from Indigenous elders to guide restoration efforts.

**Impact** – These combined efforts help protect food supplies, support farmers and herders, and keep ecosystems healthy. The projects show that restoration works best when local communities are part of the solution, using both modern science and traditional wisdom. This approach helps prevent land from becoming barren deserts, which would threaten millions of people’s livelihoods.

**What’s next step** – The issue of rangeland degradation will be discussed at a United Nations conference on desertification in Mongolia in August. The hope is that more countries will adopt similar community-driven restoration plans. Programs like the UN Development Programme’s Nature Pledge will continue to support these efforts.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Protecting and restoring rangelands depends on combining scientific data with the knowledge of the people who live there to keep ecosystems and communities strong.
articles.personality_title_fr: Communautés et données unies pour sauver les pâturages essentiels dans le monde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les pâturages sont des prairies, des broussailles et des terres arides présentes sur tous les continents sauf l'Antarctique. Ils ne sont pas cultivés comme des champs classiques, mais ils sont essentiels pour nourrir le bétail et soutenir les moyens de subsistance d'environ 2 milliards de personnes dans le monde.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Au Botswana, au Kazakhstan et au Kenya, les pâturages rétrécissent ou se dégradent à cause de la sécheresse, des plantes envahissantes et des activités humaines. Chaque pays a lancé de grands projets combinant données scientifiques et savoirs locaux pour comprendre et restaurer ces terres. Le Botswana a impliqué plus de 2 000 experts et leaders locaux pour évaluer son écosystème. Le Kazakhstan replante des arbres et améliore les pâturages sur le lit asséché de la mer d'Aral. Le Kenya utilise 33 ans de données satellites et les récits des anciens autochtones pour guider les efforts de restauration.

**Impact** – Ces efforts aident à protéger les ressources alimentaires, soutenir les agriculteurs et éleveurs, et maintenir des écosystèmes sains. Ces projets montrent que la restauration fonctionne mieux lorsque les communautés locales participent à la solution, en utilisant à la fois la science moderne et la sagesse traditionnelle. Cette approche aide à empêcher que les terres ne deviennent des déserts stériles, ce qui mettrait en danger les moyens de subsistance de millions de personnes.

**Prochaine étape** – Le problème de la dégradation des pâturages sera abordé lors d'une conférence des Nations Unies sur la désertification en Mongolie en août. L'espoir est que davantage de pays adoptent des plans de restauration similaires, axés sur les communautés. Des programmes comme l'Engagement Nature du Programme des Nations Unies pour le développement continueront de soutenir ces efforts.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Protéger et restaurer les pâturages dépend de la combinaison des données scientifiques avec les connaissances des habitants pour garder les écosystèmes et les communautés solides.
articles.personality_title_es: Comunidades y datos se unen para salvar pastizales vitales en todo el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los pastizales son praderas, arbustos y tierras secas que se encuentran en todos los continentes excepto en la Antártida. No se cultivan como campos normales, pero son esenciales para alimentar al ganado y sostener la vida de cerca de 2 mil millones de personas.

**Qué pasó** – En Botsuana, Kazajistán y Kenia, los pastizales están disminuyendo o degradándose debido a la sequía, plantas invasoras y actividades humanas. Cada país inició grandes proyectos que combinan datos científicos y conocimientos locales para entender y restaurar estas tierras. Botsuana involucró a más de 2,000 expertos y líderes locales para evaluar su ecosistema. Kazajistán está replantando árboles y mejorando pastizales en el lecho seco del Mar de Aral. Kenia usa 33 años de datos satelitales junto con historias de ancianos indígenas para guiar la restauración.

**Impacto** – Estos esfuerzos ayudan a proteger la comida, apoyar a agricultores y pastores, y mantener ecosistemas saludables. Los proyectos muestran que la restauración funciona mejor cuando las comunidades locales participan, usando ciencia moderna y sabiduría tradicional. Esta forma ayuda a evitar que las tierras se conviertan en desiertos, lo que pondría en riesgo la vida de millones.

**Próximo paso** – El problema de la degradación de los pastizales se discutirá en una conferencia de la ONU sobre desertificación en Mongolia en agosto. La esperanza es que más países adopten planes similares centrados en las comunidades. Programas como el Compromiso con la Naturaleza del Programa de Desarrollo de la ONU seguirán apoyando estos esfuerzos.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Proteger y restaurar los pastizales depende de combinar datos científicos con el conocimiento de quienes viven allí para mantener fuertes los ecosistemas y las comunidades.
